title: The First Quarter Review: What a Fractional CFO Actually Checks When September Ends
excerpt: The first quarter of FY27 closes on 30 September. Here is what a proper review of that quarter actually looks at, and why waiting until the half year to check it costs more to fix.
content:
Thirty September marks the end of the first quarter of the new financial year for most Australian SMEs, and it lands in the same fortnight as Small Business Month and the tail end of spring's early trading pickup. Three months of FY27 trading data now exists. For businesses that set a plan in July, this is the first real point where that plan can be checked against what actually happened.

Most owner-led businesses don't do anything formal with that moment. The bookkeeper closes the quarter's BAS, the numbers get filed, and attention moves straight to whatever is busiest in October. That's a reasonable use of a bookkeeper's time, because BAS lodgement and compliance reporting is exactly the job they're doing well. It isn't the same job as asking whether the business is tracking to plan, and by the time that question gets asked at the half year, three more months of drift have usually piled on top of the first three.

This is the specific moment a fractional CFO earns the retainer. Not the pitch deck moment, but the quiet ninety day check that catches a small variance while it's still a small variance.

Why the First Quarter Is the Cheapest Time to Catch a Drift

A gap between plan and actual is a different problem depending on when it's found. At the three month mark, a variance is usually still one or two decisions wide: a price hasn't moved the way it should have, a cost line has crept up since the July wage increases, a new hire hasn't yet reached the productivity the plan assumed. Any of these is fixable in the next quarter without much disruption. At the six month mark the same variance has compounded through two more quarters of trading, and closing the same gap by year end usually needs a bigger, more disruptive fix. At nine months, in many cases, the year's outcome is effectively locked in and the conversation shifts from correction to damage control.

The pattern we see across owner-led businesses is that the first quarter review gets skipped, not because anyone decided it wasn't worth doing, but because nobody carved out the fortnight to do it properly while everything else was also demanding attention. The irony is that a Q1 review is also the cheapest one to run, because there are only three months of data to reconcile rather than six or nine, and the resulting to-do list is short enough to action alongside normal trading.

What Actually Gets Reviewed in a Q1 Check

A proper first quarter review looks at three things together, not in isolation. The first is revenue and gross margin against the annual plan, broken down enough to show whether a shortfall or surplus is coming from volume, price, or mix. The second is the cash conversion picture, specifically whether debtor days and payment timing are tracking the way the plan assumed, because a business can be on budget for revenue and still be quietly falling behind on cash. The third is the cost base, checking that the July wage increases, any new supplier pricing, and any new hires are actually landing where the plan expected them to.

None of these three checks is complicated on its own. What's harder is holding all three in view at the same time, because a business can look healthy on any single measure while the combination is quietly moving the wrong way, for instance solid revenue growth sitting alongside a gross margin that's drifted down half a point and debtor days that have crept out by a week. Individually each looks minor. Together, over a full year, they change the result materially.

A structured quarterly review against the plan, with variance analysis and a short list of forward risks and opportunities, is built for exactly this moment. It turns three months of raw transaction data into a page an owner can act on in an afternoon, rather than a spreadsheet that takes a week to properly interpret.

Reviewing the Numbers Is Not the Same as Acting on Them

The review itself isn't the valuable part. What matters is what changes for the second quarter because of it: a price adjustment, a staffing decision brought forward or delayed, a cash buffer topped up before it's needed rather than after. Businesses that treat the Q1 review as a genuine planning input, rather than a historical report, are the ones that reach June with a result that resembles what they actually set out to achieve back in July. That habit of checking and adjusting every quarter, rather than once a year, is also what keeps a disciplined cash flow rhythm intact through the rest of the year.

For businesses that already have a fractional CFO partnership in place, this quarter's review is simply part of the existing rhythm. For businesses running the numbers alone, the end of September is a reasonable moment to build that rhythm before the gap between plan and actual has three more months to grow.

faqs.q: Why does the end of the first quarter matter for an Australian SME's financial plan?
faqs.a: Thirty September is the first point in the financial year where a full quarter of trading data exists against the annual plan set in July. Variances are still small and cheap to correct at this stage. Left until the half year, the same gaps have usually compounded through two more quarters of trading, and the fix needed to close them by June is bigger and more disruptive.

faqs.q: What does a quarterly business review actually look at for an SME?
faqs.a: A proper quarterly review holds three things in view together: revenue and gross margin against plan, the cash conversion picture including debtor days, and whether the cost base is moving the way it was expected to. A structured quarterly review against the plan turns that into a short, actionable list rather than a raw spreadsheet.

faqs.q: How is a fractional CFO's quarterly review different from a bookkeeper's reports?
faqs.a: A bookkeeper's reporting is built for compliance, accuracy and lodgement, and it's doing exactly the job it should. A quarterly review asks a different question: is the business tracking to the plan it set, and what needs to change next quarter if it isn't. Both roles matter, they just aren't the same job.

faqs.q: What early warning signs does a first quarter financial review usually pick up?
faqs.a: The signals are rarely dramatic on their own. A gross margin that's drifted down half a point, debtor days creeping out by a week, or a cost line that's crept up since July's wage increases. None of these looks urgent in isolation. Reviewed together after three months, they show whether the year is genuinely on track.

faqs.q: How often should an Australian SME formally review actual results against budget?
faqs.a: Quarterly is the practical minimum for most owner-led businesses, with September, December, March and June as natural checkpoints that line up with the financial year. Reviewing only at the half year or the full year means six to twelve months of drift can build up before anyone actually looks at it.

faqs.q: Does a fractional CFO only get involved when a business is already in trouble?
faqs.a: No, and that's often the more valuable use of the role. A fractional CFO partnership is usually most effective as a steady quarterly rhythm that catches small variances early, rather than a response brought in once a bigger problem has already taken hold of the business.

faqs.q: What happens if a business skips its first quarter financial review entirely?
faqs.a: Nothing happens immediately, which is exactly why it's easy to skip. The cost shows up later, when a small pricing or cost drift that could have been corrected in October has had six more months to compound, and the adjustment needed by June is larger and harder to make without disrupting the business.
